transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-30 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Liam O'Connor (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Rivera (Redwood Product); Jordan Lee (Aster PM), Maya Patel (Aster SRE), Omar Khan (Aster CTO), Tessa Rivera (Aster Legal)

Summary: Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics—streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry and backoff strategies; console quick tour and Optimize suggestions for latency/cost tradeoffs. Customer has production timeline Q1, wants predictable latency SLOs and SOC2 artifacts.

Topics covered: Hosted API streaming, response chunking, idempotency/clientside retries, batching vs single-shot calls, parameter defaults, console observability, Optimize recommendations (batching, cached prefixes), security and compliance notes.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Liam (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then we'll jump into a short live demo. I'm Liam, AE at Redwood. Priya our SE will walk through the technical bits.
[00:00:24] Jordan (PM): Hey, Jordan here. Appreciate it. We run a patient triage assistant at Aster, mostly short-turn conversations and some longer context threads. Main asks: low p99 latency for real-time chat and cost that's predictable.
[00:00:35] Priya (SE): Great. We'll show the hosted API end-to-end, streaming behavior first, then console ops and Optimize suggestions for cost.
[00:01:12] Maya (SRE): Quick note — we need SOC2 evidence, SSO integration details, and ideally a way to run a private deployment in our VPC if necessary.
[00:01:27] Liam: Yep, we'll surface security docs after. Private option exists but we'll talk hosted defaults today.
[00:02:03] Priya: Launching the demo—this is the Chat endpoint. When you call /v1/chat with streaming, the server sends tokens as they're generated. That gives you lower time-to-first-byte compared to waiting for the whole response.
[00:02:41] Priya: (screen) See here: streaming mode uses SSE-like events; our SDK provides helpers to rehydrate partial messages so you can render progressively.
[00:03:20] Jordan: How often are chunks sent? Is that configurable?
[00:03:34] Priya: Good question. Chunk cadence depends on model decode speed and tokenization. You can control model max_tokens, and we expose generation settings like temperature and top_p, but chunk size itself is a function of model and runtime.
[00:04:02] Priya: We also have a setting for stream buffer flush—it's an SDK-level option to smooth UI updates so you don't get hundred tiny frames.
[00:04:33] Maya: For our mobile app we care about bandwidth — do you support delta-only streaming to reduce payloads?
[00:04:47] Priya: Yes, by default payloads are incremental tokens only. If you want full message snapshots each event, that's configurable but will increase bandwidth.
[00:05:10] Omar (CTO): Can we pin a particular model version? We need to ensure deterministic outputs across time.
[00:05:22] Marco (Product): Absolutely—model pinning and versioning are first-class. You can specify model_id and exact revision in requests or pin at the project/route level in the Console.
[00:05:58] Jordan: What's the retry behavior if a stream cuts mid-message? We saw a couple of partials in our POC with another provider.
[00:06:18] Priya: Two strategies: client-side retry with idempotency keys and server fallback. For short interruptions we recommend resumable streaming using a message cursor—our SDK surfaces a reconnect helper that requests remaining tokens. For hard failures we suggest a full retry with the same idempotency token; the platform deduplicates on server side.
[00:06:55] Priya: There's also automatic fallback to a lower-capacity variant if the primary model is rate-limited—configurable in routing policies.
[00:07:30] Tessa (Legal): On data retention, what's logged and for how long?
[00:07:44] Liam: Hosted API retains minimal request metadata for billing and observability. For content retention we have defaults but customers can request shorter retention or opt-out; enterprise contracts cover retention, audit logs, and bring-your-own-key. We'll send the SOC2 and data-flow doc.
[00:08:20] Jordan: Great. Could you walk through a param tuning example for dialog safety vs creativity?
[00:08:36] Priya: Sure—temperature controls randomness (0.0 is deterministic). top_p trims the tail probability mass. For safety we generally set temperature 0.0–0.2 and top_p 0.8–0.95, and use system prompts + safety filters. For triage you probably want 0.0–0.1.
[00:09:10] Priya: Also max_output_tokens limits worst-case cost. If you expect short answers set max_tokens low and use follow-up calls for longer context.
[00:09:45] Jordan: Speaking of cost, how do we balance throughput vs per-token price?
[00:09:58] Marco: Two levers—batching (on Dedicated or via our Optimize recommendations) and prefix caching. Batching groups concurrent prompts to better utilize GPU, reducing per-token cost at the expense of latency. For conversational UI you prioritize low latency and use small batch sizes. Optimize will suggest per-route profiles based on your traffic pattern.
[00:10:32] Maya: Does batching harm p99?
[00:10:40] Priya: It can if you wait to accumulate a batch. We support continuous batching (non-blocking) where the runtime decides when to flush based on latency SLOs—so you get most of the benefit without large p99 impacts.
[00:11:05] Jordan: Can you show Console dashboards for per-route latency and token breakdown?
[00:11:18] Priya: Switching to Console—here's per-route latency view, token cost per request, and a timeline of model variants. You can set alerts on p95/p99 and see traces for slow requests.
[00:11:50] Priya: (screen) There's also a token-level cost heatmap so you can identify prompts that cause high costs—super useful to tune prompts.
[00:12:22] Jordan: Nice. For our infra team, how does autoscaling behave under sudden bursts?
[00:12:35] Marco: Hosted has instance pools with scale-out policies; we also offer burst capacity for short spikes. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated where you reserve GPUs. Hosted will try to route to other regions or fallback models if capacity is constrained.
[00:13:05] Omar: If routing to a different model variant happens, how do we keep output quality consistent?
[00:13:18] Priya: You configure compatible fallback variants and calibrate them with evaluation prompts. Console shows quality deltas per variant and we surface expected latency/cost tradeoffs. You can also enforce strict no-fallback for critical paths.
[00:13:50] Jordan: We use a health-check loop; if the platform falls back we want to be alerted.
[00:13:58] Liam: Alerts are configurable per-route with webhook integrations to PagerDuty/Slack.
[00:14:22] Maya: Can you demo a retry scenario?
[00:14:30] Priya: Sure—I'll simulate a transient network drop. (short pause) The SDK reconnects and requests remaining tokens. You see here the reconnect call with the idempotency key; server returns remaining content. If reconnect fails, client retries the whole request and server dedups to avoid double spend.
[00:15:10] Priya: Note: for semantic idempotency you should include a conversation id + message index.
[00:15:35] Jordan: Are there best practices for client-side debounce/throttling to protect p95?
[00:15:46] Priya: Yes—use local rate-limiting and exponential backoff with jitter. We recommend starting with a small burst allowance and exponential backoff capped at a few seconds for interactive apps.
[00:16:12] Tessa: On compliance—SSO and RBAC details?
[00:16:22] Liam: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC in Console. For Private deployments we can plug into your KMS/HSM for key management.
[00:16:50] Maya: Can we bring the inference plane into our VPC?
[00:16:58] Marco: Yes—Private offers VPC and on-prem options. It comes with an enterprise license and support SLA. We'll attach the private deployment checklist in the follow-up.
[00:17:30] Jordan: What's the onboarding timeline typically to get from PoC to production?
[00:17:42] Liam: For hosted, you can be in production within 2–4 weeks given integration and evaluation. Dedicated/private can take 6–12 weeks depending on procurement and infra.
[00:17:59] Jordan: Budget-wise, examples would help.
[00:18:08] Marco: We'll send a tailored pricing scenario showing hosted per-token vs Dedicated reserved capacity with break-even analysis.
[00:18:30] Priya: Quick note on Optimize—it will recommend quantization profiles and batching policies based on your workload. For short chats it often suggests lower batch sizes and prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[00:18:55] Priya: Also, we run automated evals against your prompt set to detect regressions on model rollouts.
[00:19:20] Maya: Can you share an example of an eval report?
[00:19:28] Priya: (screen) Here's a sample eval—per-prompt accuracy, hallucination rate, latency distribution. You can set guardrails to prevent rollout if quality drops beyond a threshold.
[00:19:58] Jordan: Ok, next I'd like to understand the SDK integration pattern for React web + mobile.
[00:20:08] Priya: We have JS SDK with streaming helpers and native mobile wrappers. The pattern: open stream for TTFB, render partials, maintain conversation state client-side, and send only deltas for follow-ups.
[00:20:40] Priya: We also provide server-side proxy patterns if you want to keep keys off the client.
[00:21:05] Omar: Any pitfalls you see with our current plan? (they described earlier—short-turn convos, some long threads)
[00:21:17] Priya: Two: unbounded context growth (cache or truncate early) and not guarding max_tokens which can spike cost. Use per-conversation prefix caching for repeated info and set a hard max_token budget per message.
[00:21:45] Jordan: Can Optimize recommend a truncation heuristic?
[00:21:52] Marco: Yes—we can tune based on signal like token reuse and relevance; Optimize surfaces suggested window sizes.
[00:22:20] Maya: For our security team—where can they see audit logs?
[00:22:30] Liam: Console -> Compliance -> Audit logs. For Private deployments you get additional wire-level logs and HSM integration.
[00:22:55] Tessa: Will your contract include indemnities around model outputs?
[00:23:02] Liam: Standard enterprise language—we'll route legal questions, but we do offer tailored clauses. We'll loop legal on both sides.
[00:23:25] Jordan: Walk me through an example latency-cost tradeoff: same prompt, two models, one faster but more expensive.
[00:23:36] Priya: (screen) Here are two variants—Model-A (low latency, high cost) and Model-B (slower, cheaper). Console sim shows expected p95 and per-token cost. You can set policy to use Model-A for logged-in users and Model-B for background processing.
[00:24:12] Jordan: Any recommendation for fallbacks on intermittent high load?
[00:24:20] Priya: Use a tiered routing policy: primary fast model, fallback cheap model, and last-resort cached responses for repetitive prompts. Also alert on variant drift so you can decide to pause fallbacks.
[00:24:48] Maya: About billing — are tokens rounded per request or per-1000?
[00:24:57] Marco: Per-token with per-1k granularity on invoices; Console exposes token counts by route so you can reconcile.
[00:25:25] Jordan: Great. Let's talk about a short technical deep dive next week focused on Maya's performance tests.
[00:25:33] Liam: Sounds good — we'll propose a slot.
[00:25:45] Priya: Final quick demo—I'll show a code snippet for streaming with reconnect + idempotency. (reads snippet) Note the idempotency header and conversation_id in metadata.
[00:26:20] Priya: Also note we include server-sent progress events for attachments like images or tool-calls.
[00:26:50] Jordan: Do you support function calling / structured outputs?
[00:26:58] Priya: Yes—we support function/tool calling with schema validation. Console also shows a structured output inspector.
[00:27:22] Omar: I'm curious about cold-start latency—how fast are responses for the first request?
[00:27:33] Priya: Cold-starts vary by model size. For our medium variants typical TTFB is 80–160ms, large models can be 200–400ms. We reduce variance with continuous warm pools and weighted routing.
[00:28:05] Maya: Any recommendations for mobile offline degrade?
[00:28:12] Priya: Use local heuristics to show cached snippets or partial answers and queue retries. For critical flows implement server-side fallbacks that return precomputed responses.
[00:28:45] Jordan: Ok let's recap and actions.
[00:28:52] Liam: Recap: 1) we'll send SOC2 + SSO docs and private deployment checklist; 2) pricing scenarios and latency/cost spreadsheet; 3) Priya will run a 1k-message L7 latency test with their sample prompts; 4) schedule a Maya-led deep technical session.
[00:29:25] Tessa: Legal will review docs once received.
[00:29:33] Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:29:40] Liam: Thanks — we'll follow up via email with links.
[00:30:00] (meeting wrap, some side chatter about calendar invites)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings on product names (we said continuity batching vs continuous batching), and some tokens garbled during demo—full logs attached in follow-up.
